Q: Python Requests throwing "SSLError" A:

In case you have a library that relies on Requests and you cannot modify the verify path (like with pyvmomi) then you'll have to find the cacert.pem file bundled with Requests and append your CA there. Here's a generic approach to find the cacert.pem file location:

Windows

python -c "import requests; print requests.certs.where()"

Output:

c:\Python27\lib\site-packages\requests-2.8.1-py2.7.egg\requests\cacert.pem

Linux

As root:

#  Python 2.7.5, requests 2.7.0, and verify not enforced
python -c "import requests; print requests.certs.where()"

Output:

/usr/lib/python2.7/dist-packages/certifi/cacert.pem

And:

# (Python 2.7.10, and verify enforced)
python -c "import requests; print requests.certs.where()"

Output:

/usr/local/lib/python2.7/dist-packages/requests/cacert.pem

btw. @requests-devs, bundling your own cacerts with Requests is really, really annoying... especially the fact that you do not seem to use the system CA store first and this is not documented anywhere.

update

In situations, where you're using a library and don't have any control over the ca-bundle location, you could also explicitly set the ca-bundle location to be your host-wide ca-bundle:

REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE=/etc/ssl/certs/ca-bundle.crt python -c "import requests; requests.get('https://somesite.com')";

Q: Intermittent 403 Forbidden client error response status code when scraping with Selenium A:

403 Forbidden error

The HTTP 403 Forbidden client error response status code indicates that the server has authenticated the request, but the request failed due to insufficient rights and the response body contains a reason for the failure. The request failure is tied to application logic such as insufficient permissions to a resource or action. Clients that receive a 403 response should expect that repeating the same request without any modification will fail with the same 403 error.

As an example, a HTTP 403 Forbidden client error response status code due to InsufficientPermissions will be similar to:

HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden
Date: Tue, 28 Jun 2026 12:56:49 GMT
Content-Type: application/json
Content-Length: 88

{
  "error": "InsufficientPermissions",
  "message": "Deleting users requires the 'admin' role."
}

Types of 403 Forbidden Errors

A 403 Forbidden Error is not always clear why it occurs. There are many types of 403 Forbidden Error as below:

  • 403: The most common error that occurs when the server understands the request but refuses to authorize access.
  • 403.1 Execute Access Forbidden: This occurs when the server does not allow execution of server-side scripts, executable files or CGI programs.
  • 403.2 Read Access Forbidden: This error occurs when the server prevents users from viewing or reading the requested resource.
  • 403.4 SSL Required: This error occurs when access to the resource requires a secure HTTPS connection.
  • 403.5 SSL 128 Required: This error occurs when the server requires a secure SSL connection with at least 128-bit encryption.
  • 403.6 IP Address Rejected: This error occurs when the server has blocked the user's IP address from accessing the resource.

Common Causes of 403 Forbidden Error

Some common causes when the server understands the request but denies access to the requested resource can be either of the follows:

  • Authentication Failures: Incorrect login credentials or insufficient user permissions.
  • Firewall Blocks: A web application firewall blocking the request considering as suspicious.
  • Faulty Plugins: Misconfigured or incompatible plugins restricting the access.
  • IP Blacklisting: Specific IP addresses blocked by the server or website.
  • Server Misconfigurations: Incorrect server, file, or security settings.
  • Moved or Restricted Content: The requested resource/webpage has been relocated or access-limited.
  • Legal Restrictions: Access denied due to regional or legal compliance organizational policies.
  • High Resource Demand: Heavy traffic or server overload temporarily restricting access.
  • ACL Restrictions: Access Control Lists preventing unauthorized users from accessing the sought resources.

Common Solutions

Some of the common and effective methods to fix the 403 Forbidden error are as follows:

  • Refresh the webpage verifying the URL.
  • Disable VPN & Proxy as some websites block VPN traffic for security reasons.
  • Clear the browser cache and cookies.

This usecase

As the testcases generally gets executed fine but every 10 minutes or so you are facing 403 errors you requests may be much above the throttle limit. In such a case you need to slow down your test execution.

Q: Convert raw SQL containing a subquery in the FROM clause to CodeIgniter's query builder A:

First, yes, you can implement your entire SQL using CodeIgniter's query builder methods (at least in CodeIgniter 3 - the only version I've ever used).

return $this->db
    ->from(
        '('
        . $this->db
            ->order_by('created_at', 'desc')
            ->get_compiled_select('inbox')
        . ') query'
    )
    ->group_by('id')
    ->get()
    ->result();

Or separate the subquery as a variable:

$sub = $this->db
    ->order_by('created_at', 'desc')
    ->get_compiled_select('inbox');

return $this->db
    ->group_by('id')
    ->get("($sub) query")
    ->result();

Now, for the sanity check!

It looks like you are trying to fetch rows for each unique id with data containing the most recent / greatest created_at value.

Your implementation is evidently not reliable because the sorting in the subquery is prone to being lost in the parent query's result.

Instead, your query can be refactored a number of ways depending on your database dialect and version to return a reliabale result set. Here are a few examples and the SQLize Demo:

  • Window function syntax:

    SELECT id, created_at, val
FROM (
    SELECT
        *,
        ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY id ORDER BY created_at DESC) rn
    FROM inbox
) sub
WHERE rn = 1;

    CodeIgniter query builder:

    $sub = $this->db
    ->select()
    ->select('ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY id ORDER BY created_at DESC) rn')
    ->get_compiled_select('inbox')

return $this->db
    ->select('id, created_at, val')
    ->get_where("($sub) sub", ['rn' => 1])
    ->result();



  • Filter the table data by JOINing only on the latest rows per id:

    SELECT i.*
FROM inbox i
JOIN (
    SELECT id, MAX(created_at) created_at
    FROM inbox
    GROUP BY id
) latest USING (id, created_at);

    CodeIgniter query builder:

    $sub = $this->db
    ->select('id')
    ->select_max('created_at')
    ->group_by('id')
    ->get_compiled_select('inbox');

return $this->db
    ->select('i.*')
    ->join("($sub) sub", 'id, created_at')
    ->get_where('inbox, i')
    ->result();



  • WHERE id and created_at match the latest row per id:

    SELECT *
FROM inbox i
WHERE created_at = (
    SELECT created_at
    FROM inbox sub
    WHERE sub.id = i.id
    ORDER BY created_at DESC
    LIMIT 1
)

    CodeIgniter query builder:

    $sub = $this->db
    ->select('created_at')
    ->where('sub.id = i.id')
    ->order_by('created_at', 'desc')
    ->limit(1)
    ->get_compiled_select('inbox sub');

return $this->db
    ->where('created_at', "($sub)", false)
    ->get('inbox i');

    or

    return $this->db->get_where(
    'inbox i',
    sprintf(
        'created_at = (%s)',
        $this->db
            ->select('created_at')
            ->where('sub.id = i.id')
            ->order_by('created_at', 'desc')
            ->limit(1)
            ->get_compiled_select('inbox sub')
    )
);
